entry.englishMeaning: the specialized vocabulary used in a field
entry.coreIdea: The specialised words used in a field.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract noun for the specialized words used in a subject or profession.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral: specialized vocabulary can be useful or confusing depending on the audience; the word does not itself criticize jargon.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Explanatory and cautionary here: changing applicants' wording is presented as a possible reason for model performance to decline.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Neutral to formal; common in education and professional discussion. “The terms people use” is a plainer explanation.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: For example, if a new wave of applicants start using different resume formats or terminology, the model might start to degrade.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: the specialized vocabulary used in a field
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The source says that changes in the terms applicants use could affect a model trained on earlier resume wording.

when_to_use: Discuss the specialised vocabulary used in a profession, subject or activity.
when_not_to_use: Do not use terminology for the full grammar or writing style of a document; it concerns the terms used.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: the terminology of + field; technical terminology; use / explain + terminology
common_collocations: technical terminology
medical terminology

examples.example_1: The course explains the terminology used in software testing.
examples.example_2: She asked the instructor to explain the unfamiliar gardening terminology.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: I understand the idea, but not these words.
B: Let us go through the terminology first.
A: That will make the instructions easier to follow.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: This paragraph contains several difficult terminologies, when referring to individual words.
mistakes_differences.correction: Say: This paragraph contains several difficult terms, or some difficult terminology.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Terminology refers collectively to specialised terms; a term is one particular word or expression within that vocabulary.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: A short glossary collects the words used by one profession.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: Please explain the terminology before demonstrating the equipment.
memory_practice.recall_question: Would you normally call three specialised expressions three terms or three terminologies?
memory_practice.recognition_task: A: The specialised names for parts of an engine. B: The paragraph's punctuation. Which is terminology?
memory_practice.production_task: Explain one piece of terminology from your work to a newcomer, then give its plain-English meaning.

advanced_nuance: Terminology is not automatically a criticism. Jargon often suggests that specialised wording is difficult or unnecessary for the audience; terminology can describe that vocabulary neutrally.

entry.coreIdea: Something happens occasionally without a fixed schedule.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Time expression meaning occasionally, with intervals between events; no fixed schedule is implied.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral: it describes how often something happens without judging whether that frequency is enough.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Relaxed and matter-of-fact here: the speaker describes occasional coffee meetings.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common conversational English. “Occasionally” is more compact and somewhat more formal.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: We meet for coffee every now and then.
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The speakers meet for coffee from time to time, rather than at a stated regular interval.

when_to_use: Describe occasional visits, actions or events when the precise frequency is unimportant or irregular.
when_not_to_use: For a fixed weekly appointment, say every week rather than using this vague occasional expression.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: every now and then + clause; clause + every now and then
common_collocations: meet every now and then
check in every now and then

examples.example_1: We meet for coffee every now and then.
examples.example_2: Every now and then, I take the longer route home through the park.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Do you still see your old neighbours?
B: Every now and then. We sometimes meet at the market.
A: It is nice to stay in touch.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Mistake: Using every now and then to promise an exact weekly update.
mistakes_differences.correction: Use every week for that commitment. Every now and then means occasionally and gives no fixed interval.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Every now and then means occasionally; every other day means once every two days. The latter specifies a schedule.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: A few scattered dots on a calendar instead of a repeated appointment.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: I check the old photo album every now and then.
memory_practice.recall_question: Does every now and then tell the listener exactly when the next event will happen?
memory_practice.recognition_task: A: An occasional unscheduled coffee. B: A meeting every Monday at ten. Which better fits every now and then?
memory_practice.production_task: Describe something enjoyable you do every now and then, without inventing a fixed timetable.

advanced_nuance: Every now and then is conversational and deliberately approximate. The actual gap may be days or months; the activity and surrounding context determine what counts as occasional.

entry.pronunciation: Approximate pronunciation: SNAP. Capitals show stress; this is text guidance, not audio.
entry.englishMeaning: to speak to someone suddenly in an angry or impatient way
entry.coreIdea: Speak suddenly and sharply because you are angry or impatient.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Figurative verb for speaking sharply and suddenly in anger or impatience, rather than describing a physical break.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Negative here: it presents the speaker's manner as hurtful or unpleasant.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Critical and warning here: “self-defeating” and the effect on the loved one explain why repeated sharp remarks cause trouble.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common in everyday speech and narrative. “Spoke sharply” is a more explicit description for a formal account.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: "  Unf ortunately  (and here's  where  the  problem  becomes  self­ defeati ng) ,  the  more  you  snip  and  snap,  the  less  your  loved  one  wants  to  be  around  you.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: to speak to someone suddenly in an angry or impatient way
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The passage warns that repeated sharp remarks make a loved one less willing to be around the speaker.

when_to_use: Describe a brief, angry or impatient spoken response.
when_not_to_use: For a firm but calm statement, use say firmly rather than snap unless the sharpness is intended.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: snap at + person; snap + quoted words; snap back at + person
common_collocations: snap at someone
snap an impatient reply

examples.example_1: Please do not snap at me; I am only asking where the keys are.
examples.example_2: She was tempted to snap back, but paused before answering.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Where did you put the folder?
B: Stop asking me!
A: There is no need to snap at me. I just need it for the meeting.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: He snapped to me when I asked a question, when describing an angry response.
mistakes_differences.correction: Say: He snapped at me when I asked a question. Use at for the person receiving the sharp response.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Snap focuses on a sudden sharp reply; shout focuses on loudness. Someone can snap in a low voice.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: A short reply lands with a sharp edge.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: I try not to snap at people when I am tired.
memory_practice.recall_question: Does someone have to speak loudly to snap at another person?
memory_practice.recognition_task: A: A brief impatient answer. B: A loud cheerful greeting across a field. Which better fits snap?
memory_practice.production_task: Write a short exchange where someone almost snaps at a colleague, then chooses a calmer response.

advanced_nuance: Snap often suggests a moment when patience gives way, but it does not excuse the impact of the remark. The source emphasises the cumulative effect of repeated sharp responses on a relationship.

entry.pronunciation: Approximate pronunciation: NAW at. Capitals show stress; this is text guidance, not audio.
entry.englishMeaning: to cause persistent worry, discomfort, or distress
entry.coreIdea: A worry keeps troubling you instead of fading away.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Figurative phrasal verb for persistent worry, pictured as something repeatedly biting or wearing at a person.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Negative: it emphasizes an ongoing mental discomfort rather than a passing thought.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Reflective and probing here: the question asks readers to identify the conversations that trouble them most.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Expressive vocabulary in conversation and personal writing. “Keep worrying you” is a simpler alternative.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: What  are  the  specific  conversations  that  gnaw  at  you  the  most?
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: to cause persistent worry, discomfort, or distress
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The question asks which conversations cause the reader the most persistent mental discomfort.

when_to_use: Describe recurring guilt, doubt or worry that continues to disturb someone.
when_not_to_use: For a passing thought that causes no distress, use occur to or cross your mind instead.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: worry / doubt / guilt + gnaw at + person; something continues to gnaw at someone
common_collocations: doubt began to gnaw at him
guilt continued to gnaw at her

examples.example_1: The unanswered question continued to gnaw at me throughout the weekend.
examples.example_2: Doubts about the decision began to gnaw at her after the meeting.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Why are you still thinking about yesterday's conversation?
B: My careless comment keeps gnawing at me.
A: You could contact her and explain what you meant.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Missing the usual preposition: The doubt gnawed me all evening. For the expression taught here, keep at.
mistakes_differences.correction: Say: The doubt gnawed at me all evening. Keep at in this expression.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Gnaw at suggests persistent, wearing discomfort; surprise describes a sudden reaction that may pass quickly.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: One unresolved worry keeps nibbling at your attention.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: The thought of the unfinished apology continued to gnaw at me.
memory_practice.recall_question: What makes gnaw at stronger than simply think about?
memory_practice.recognition_task: A: A worry repeatedly returns and makes someone uneasy. B: A neutral idea appears once and is forgotten. Which gnaws at the person?
memory_practice.production_task: Describe an invented unresolved concern that gnaws at someone and a constructive step they could take.

advanced_nuance: Gnaw at presents worry as gradually wearing on a person. It often works well with continue, keep or begin because those words show the persistence or development of the feeling.

entry.pronunciation: Approximate pronunciation: kawt ON KWIK-lee. Capitals show stress; this is text guidance, not audio.
entry.coreIdea: Understood what to do after little time or explanation.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract phrasal verb meaning to understand or learn; “quickly” describes how little time the learning took.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Positive here: fast understanding is presented as an ability of the pig.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Approving and lightly affectionate here: “although tiny” introduces a contrast with the pig's appetite and ability to learn.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common conversational English and accessible narrative. In a formal learning report, “learned quickly” is more direct.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: pig, although tiny, had a good appetite and caught on quickly.
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The small pig learned or understood quickly. Caught on describes learning, and quickly describes the speed.

when_to_use: Describe someone who soon understands an explanation, procedure or way of doing something.
when_not_to_use: Do not use caught on quickly merely to mean physically catching an object; this is the understanding sense.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: subject + caught on quickly; caught on quickly to + idea / procedure
common_collocations: caught on quickly to the rules
caught on quickly after a demonstration

examples.example_1: The new volunteer caught on quickly after watching one demonstration.
examples.example_2: My grandfather caught on quickly to the rules of the card game.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Did you have to explain the game many times?
B: No, she caught on quickly.
A: Great. She can join the next round.

mistakes_differences.correction: Say: He caught on quickly. Caught is the past tense of catch.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Caught on quickly means understood quickly; memorised quickly means retained information quickly. Understanding and memorising are related but different.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: One demonstration is enough for the learner to say, I see how it works.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: She caught on quickly and completed the next step herself.
memory_practice.recall_question: What did the learner do quickly in caught on quickly?
memory_practice.recognition_task: A: Understand the rules after a short explanation. B: Repeat the words without understanding them. Which better fits caught on quickly?
memory_practice.production_task: Describe someone learning a new everyday task. Use caught on quickly and explain what showed their understanding.

advanced_nuance: Caught on quickly is conversational and approving in the source. It reports quick understanding, not necessarily complete mastery or flawless performance afterward.

entry.englishMeaning: used to give a brief summary of the main point

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Discourse marker introducing a brief summary: the essential point is that more evidence is needed before commitment.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral: it signals compression, not approval or rejection by itself.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Concise and cautious here: the summary postpones commitment until there is stronger evidence.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Neutral; natural in conversation, presentations and written summaries. It should introduce a real summary rather than an unrelated new point.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: In short, we need more evidence before committing.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: used to give a brief summary of the main point
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The speaker summarises the position: the group needs additional evidence before making a commitment.

when_to_use: Condense a preceding explanation into its essential message.
when_not_to_use: Do not introduce an unrelated new topic with in short; the phrase promises a summary of what matters in the discussion.

common_collocations: in short, we need more time
in short, the plan is workable

examples.example_1: In short, we need more evidence before committing.
examples.example_2: In short, the flat suits us, but the rent is too high.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: There are extra fees, the train is infrequent, and the hotel is far away.
B: So what is your recommendation?
A: In short, we should choose another venue.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Mistake: Using in short and then repeating every detail of the earlier explanation.
mistakes_differences.correction: After in short, give the central point: In short, we cannot meet that date with the current team.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: In short introduces a concise summary; for example introduces an illustration, which may add detail rather than compress it.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: A long page of notes becomes one clear sentence.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: In short, the repairs will cost more than we expected.
memory_practice.recall_question: What should the listener expect after in short?
memory_practice.recognition_task: A: The essential conclusion in one sentence. B: A new unrelated anecdote. Which belongs after in short?
memory_practice.production_task: Write two sentences describing a scheduling problem, then summarise them with in short.

advanced_nuance: In short can summarise a practical conclusion as well as restate earlier facts. The conclusion should still follow from the preceding discussion rather than introduce an unsupported claim.

entry.pronunciation: Approximate pronunciation: hyoo-MAN-ih-tee. Capitals show stress; this is text guidance, not audio.
entry.englishMeaning: the qualities, nature, and dignity shared by human beings
entry.coreIdea: Recognise another person's shared human dignity.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract noun for the human qualities and dignity people share; here, another person's worth as a human being.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Positive and respectful: it encourages recognition of dignity despite disagreement.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Reconciliatory here: “honor and regard” describes a way to keep dialogue possible.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Neutral to formal, common in ethical and reflective discussion. It does not mean the entire human population in this entry.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: We  can,  however,  stay  in  dialogue  by  finding  a way  to  honor  and  regard  another  person's  basic  humanity.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: the qualities, nature, and dignity shared by human beings
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The source suggests respecting the other person's basic dignity as a way to keep dialogue possible despite disagreement.

when_to_use: Discuss people's human qualities or dignity, especially when recognising the person behind a role or conflict.
when_not_to_use: Do not treat respecting someone's humanity as automatic agreement with their actions or arguments.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: respect / recognise / honour + someone's humanity; shared / basic humanity
common_collocations: our shared humanity
recognise someone's humanity

examples.example_1: The story asks us to recognise the humanity of people we disagree with.
examples.example_2: She spoke about the workers' lives to remind the audience of their shared humanity.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: I strongly disagree with his decision.
B: You can challenge it without denying his humanity.
A: I will focus on the action rather than insult him.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Mistake: Thinking that recognising someone's humanity requires approving everything they do.
mistakes_differences.correction: Recognise the person's humanity while still evaluating their actions and holding them responsible.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Humanity here means shared human dignity and qualities; agreement concerns whether you accept a particular view or decision.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Behind the job title or argument is a person with a human life.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: We can disagree while respecting each other's humanity.
memory_practice.recall_question: Can you respect someone's humanity and still challenge their behaviour?
memory_practice.recognition_task: A: Criticise an action while recognising the person's dignity. B: Describe the person as worthless. Which respects their humanity?
memory_practice.production_task: Write a sentence that firmly challenges a fictional unfair decision while preserving respect for the decision-maker's humanity.

advanced_nuance: Humanity in this entry refers to human qualities and dignity, not to the entire human population. The surrounding phrase another person's basic humanity makes the intended meaning clear.

entry.pronunciation: Approximate pronunciation: KAIR uh-BOUT thair GOHLZ. Capitals show stress; this is text guidance, not audio.
entry.englishMeaning: to consider other people’s objectives important
entry.coreIdea: Treat other people's aims as important.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract phrase for treating other people's objectives as important, rather than merely knowing what they want.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Positive here: concern for their goals is presented as part of cooperation.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Reassuring and explanatory: the passage describes how people recognize a shared purpose.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Natural in everyday and workplace English. It does not necessarily mean agreeing to every goal the other person has.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: Mutual  Purpose  means  that  others  perceive  that  we  are  working  toward  a  common  outcome  in  the   conver sation,  that  we  care  about  their  goals,  intere sts,  and  valu es.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: to consider other people’s objectives important
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The source says that a shared purpose involves other people seeing that their objectives, interests and values matter to us.

when_to_use: Explain genuine concern for the outcomes other people are trying to achieve.
when_not_to_use: Do not use the phrase as an empty assurance while ignoring their stated priorities; identify which goals you are considering.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: care about their goals; change their to your / our / her / his as the people change
common_collocations: show that you care about their goals
care about their goals and priorities

examples.example_1: We need to show the volunteers that we care about their goals as well as our deadline.
examples.example_2: When trainees explain their ambitions, good mentors show that they care about their goals.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: The volunteers think we only care about filling the rota.
B: Let us ask what they want to learn and show that we care about their goals.
A: We can include that in the next planning meeting.

mistakes_differences.correction: Say: We care about their goals. Keep about before the thing that matters to you.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Know their goals means be aware of them; care about their goals means consider them important. Awareness alone does not demonstrate concern.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Put the other person's desired outcome beside your own on the planning sheet.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: Ask questions that show you care about their goals.
memory_practice.recall_question: How is caring about their goals different from knowing what their goals are?
memory_practice.recognition_task: A: Listen to their priorities and consider them in the plan. B: Record their priorities but dismiss them without thought. Which shows concern?
memory_practice.production_task: Write a response to a colleague explaining how you care about their goals while also naming one constraint you must discuss together.

advanced_nuance: Care about their goals does not promise to satisfy every goal. It signals that those aims deserve serious consideration, including an honest discussion when goals conflict.

entry.pronunciation: Approximate pronunciation: am-BIV-uh-luhns. Capitals show stress; this is text guidance, not audio.
entry.tamilMeaning: ஒரே விஷயத்தைப் பற்றி முரண்பட்ட உணர்வுகள் கொண்டிருத்தல்
entry.englishMeaning: the state of having conflicting feelings about someone or something
entry.coreIdea: Feel pulled in different directions about the same choice.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract noun for having conflicting feelings about the same person, choice or situation.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral as a description of mixed feelings; it does not automatically imply dishonesty or indecision.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Humorous here: the invented word “bivaling” plays with the term while describing unexpected certainty about the move.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Relatively formal, used in reflective and psychological discussion. “Mixed feelings” is the everyday equivalent.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: You  expected  your  spouse  to  have  fe elings  of  ambivalence  over  the  move,  but  he  or  she  doesn't  seem  to  be  bivaling  even  a  tiny  bit.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: the state of having conflicting feelings about someone or something
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The speaker expected the spouse to have mixed feelings about moving, but describes an unexpectedly clear reaction using a playful invented word.

when_to_use: Describe simultaneous conflicting feelings about a person, decision or situation.
when_not_to_use: Do not use ambivalence merely for not caring; a person can care strongly while experiencing opposing feelings.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: ambivalence about / towards + person or choice; feelings of ambivalence
common_collocations: ambivalence about moving
express ambivalence

examples.example_1: She felt ambivalence about the promotion: the work appealed to her, but the travel did not.
examples.example_2: His ambivalence towards the old house came from loving its history while resenting its upkeep.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Are you pleased about the move?
B: I feel some ambivalence. I want the new opportunity, but I will miss my friends.
A: Both reactions make sense.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Mistake: Using ambivalence as a synonym for complete indifference.
mistakes_differences.correction: Use ambivalence for mixed or conflicting feelings; use indifference when someone does not particularly care.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Ambivalence is conflict between feelings; uncertainty is lack of a definite answer or judgement. You can know the facts and still feel ambivalent.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: One part of you leans toward the choice while another pulls back.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: I felt ambivalence about leaving a familiar place for a new opportunity.
memory_practice.recall_question: What two competing feelings create ambivalence in your example?
memory_practice.recognition_task: A: Excited by a move but sad about leaving friends. B: Uninterested in where you live. Which shows ambivalence?
memory_practice.production_task: Describe a fictional career choice that produces ambivalence. Name the appealing aspect and the concern.

advanced_nuance: Ambivalence need not produce indecision: someone can make a clear choice while retaining mixed feelings. The source's humorous bivaling is wordplay, not the standard verb to teach.

entry.englishMeaning: during the period before a later event or arrangement
entry.coreIdea: During the temporary gap before the next arrangement begins.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Time connector for the temporary period before a later arrangement begins; here, before the new manager starts.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral: it identifies a temporary interval without judging the arrangement.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Practical and reassuring here: the sentence explains who will coordinate the team during the gap.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Relatively formal, natural in workplace updates. “In the meantime” is more conversational.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: The new manager starts next month; in the interim, Priya will coordinate the team.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: during the period before a later event or arrangement
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: Priya will coordinate the team during the period before the new manager starts next month.

when_to_use: Describe a temporary action or arrangement lasting until an expected later event.
when_not_to_use: For a permanent arrangement with no relevant later transition, do not imply a temporary gap by saying in the interim.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: later event; in the interim, + temporary arrangement
common_collocations: in the interim, continue as usual
in the interim, use a temporary arrangement

examples.example_1: The new manager starts next month; in the interim, Priya will coordinate the team.
examples.example_2: The library reopens in June; in the interim, readers can use the mobile service.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: The replacement printer arrives on Friday.
B: What should we do in the interim?
A: Use the printer upstairs.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: In interim, use the upstairs room.
mistakes_differences.correction: Say: In the interim, use the upstairs room. Include the in this fixed phrase.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: In the interim refers to the intervening period; eventually refers to a later outcome, without describing what happens during the gap.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: A temporary bridge covers the gap between two settled arrangements.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: The office reopens next week; in the interim, we will work from home.
memory_practice.recall_question: Which later event marks the end of the interim period in the source?
memory_practice.recognition_task: A: A temporary coordinator serves until the manager starts. B: A role is created permanently with no planned transition. Which fits in the interim?
memory_practice.production_task: Announce a short temporary arrangement using in the interim and specify the event that will end it.

advanced_nuance: In the interim sounds more formal than in the meantime. It does not itself specify the duration, so name the later event or expected date when that matters.
